en.title: Mughal-Period Land, Revenue and Agrarian Society
en.summary: Mughal rule did not replace the agrarian society of Mithila, Vajji and Anga with a single uniform land system. It superimposed imperial fiscal claims, assignments and administrative categories upon village production, regional chieftaincies, hereditary local offices and ecologies shaped by the Ganga, Gandak, Kosi and their tributaries. The most useful contemporary source, Abu’l-Fazl’s A’in-i Akbari, gives unusually detailed fiscal statistics for the Bihar subah, including the sarkars of Tirhut, Hajipur and Munger.

mai.title: मुगलकालीन भूमि, राजस्व आ कृषक समाज
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “मुगलकालीन भूमि, राजस्व आ कृषक समाज” विषयक राजस्व, व्यापार, कम्पनी शासन, नगदी फसल, अकाल, सर्वेक्षण, शिक्षा, मुद्रण, यातायात आ श्रमक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Land revenue is a social relation before it is a statistic
The subah–sarkar framework made the region fiscally legible
The A’in-i Akbari is an administrative archive, not a census
Tirhut appears as a large, internally differentiated fiscal unit

en.title: Trade between Bengal, Bihar, Nepal and the Gangetic World
en.summary: Trade connected the socio-economic worlds of Mithila, Vajji and Anga to regions far beyond their political boundaries. The Ganga formed the principal east–west trunk between the upper Gangetic plain and Bengal; Patna developed as a major inland entrepôt; Munger and Bhagalpur lay on the eastern river corridor; Hajipur and Tirhut fed northward routes toward Nepal; and Kathmandu connected plains commerce with Himalayan and Tibetan exchange.

mai.title: बंगाल, बिहार, नेपाल आ गंगा-जगत बीच व्यापार
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “बंगाल, बिहार, नेपाल आ गंगा-जगत बीच व्यापार” विषयक राजस्व, व्यापार, कम्पनी शासन, नगदी फसल, अकाल, सर्वेक्षण, शिक्षा, मुद्रण, यातायात आ श्रमक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Trade is a network of movements, not a line between two capitals
The Ganga was the principal east–west transport trunk
Ralph Fitch’s journey shows an already integrated late-sixteenth-century corridor
Seventeenth-century Patna became an entrepôt rather than merely a producing town

en.title: East India Company Expansion and the Remaking of Agrarian Relations
en.summary: Between the military victories of the East India Company in the 1750s and 1760s and the Permanent Settlement of 1793 lay nearly three decades of experimentation. The decisive change was not that a wholly new agrarian order appeared overnight after Plassey or Buxar.

mai.title: ईस्ट इंडिया कम्पनीक विस्तार आ कृषक सम्बन्धक पुनर्गठन
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “ईस्ट इंडिया कम्पनीक विस्तार आ कृषक सम्बन्धक पुनर्गठन” विषयक राजस्व, व्यापार, कम्पनी शासन, नगदी फसल, अकाल, सर्वेक्षण, शिक्षा, मुद्रण, यातायात आ श्रमक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Company expansion was a sequence, not a single conquest
Buxar made Bihar central to the Company’s territorial state
The Diwani grant of 1765 changed the legal claim to revenue
“Dual government” describes divided responsibility but can conceal continuity

en.title: Permanent Settlement and Landed Society
en.summary: The Permanent Settlement of 1793 converted the experimental decennial settlement of Bengal and Bihar into a perpetual state demand upon designated zamindars, independent talukdars and other proprietors. Its importance lay not simply in fixing revenue, but in reworking the legal language of landed authority. A hereditary revenue-collecting right was increasingly treated as proprietary property, while punctual payment to the colonial state became the condition of security.

mai.title: स्थायी बन्दोबस्त आ भूमिधारी समाज
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “स्थायी बन्दोबस्त आ भूमिधारी समाज” विषयक राजस्व, व्यापार, कम्पनी शासन, नगदी फसल, अकाल, सर्वेक्षण, शिक्षा, मुद्रण, यातायात आ श्रमक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: From decennial experiment to perpetual settlement
What Regulation I of 1793 actually fixed
Zamindar as proprietor: a colonial legal translation
Property rights were tied to revenue responsibility

en.title: Indigo and Commercial Agriculture
en.summary: Indigo was one of the clearest ways in which colonial commercial agriculture entered the agrarian society created under permanent settlement. The crop linked cultivators and labourers in Bihar to European capital, Calcutta agency houses, factory processing, long-distance transport and volatile international dye markets. Yet the system was not uniform. Indigo could be grown directly on factory-controlled land, by tenants under advance-and-contract arrangements, or by independent cultivators.

mai.title: नील आ वाणिज्यिक कृषि
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “नील आ वाणिज्यिक कृषि” विषयक राजस्व, व्यापार, कम्पनी शासन, नगदी फसल, अकाल, सर्वेक्षण, शिक्षा, मुद्रण, यातायात आ श्रमक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Indigo as commodity, dye and agrarian institution
European indigo expansion in eastern India
Capital, agency houses and seasonal finance
Permanent settlement and access to landed rights

en.title: Opium and Other Commodity Networks
en.summary: Opium turned Bihar into one of the most tightly regulated commodity landscapes of the British Empire. Yet the poppy was never the whole economy. Cultivators in Mithila, Vajji and Anga also produced grain, oilseeds, tobacco, sugarcane and indigo; specialist workers made and refined saltpetre; Bhagalpur sustained silk and tasar manufacture; lac and other forest-linked products moved through eastern markets.

mai.title: अफीम आ अन्य वस्तु-जाल
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “अफीम आ अन्य वस्तु-जाल” विषयक राजस्व, व्यापार, कम्पनी शासन, नगदी फसल, अकाल, सर्वेक्षण, शिक्षा, मुद्रण, यातायात आ श्रमक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Opium as a commodity system rather than a single crop
Patna had an opium economy before Company monopoly
From political conquest to commercial monopoly
The 1773 contract regime concentrated control

en.title: Famines, Scarcity and Food Security
en.summary: Scarcity has repeatedly exposed the relationship between ecology, markets, household resources and public authority in Mithila, Vajji and Anga. A failed monsoon or damaged rice crop could begin a crisis, but famine emerged only when households lost effective access to food: grain prices rose faster than wages, cattle and tools were sold, seed was eaten, credit contracted, employment failed, or transport could not move food from surplus to deficit areas.

mai.title: अकाल, अभाव आ खाद्य-सुरक्षा
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “अकाल, अभाव आ खाद्य-सुरक्षा” विषयक राजस्व, व्यापार, कम्पनी शासन, नगदी फसल, अकाल, सर्वेक्षण, शिक्षा, मुद्रण, यातायात आ श्रमक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Famine is a social process, not simply a failed harvest
Food security had four linked dimensions: harvest, market, household and state
The regional ecology produced both abundance and recurrent risk
Grain prices were often a more immediate danger to the poor than aggregate shortage

en.title: Colonial Surveys and the Invention of Social Categories
en.summary: Colonial surveys created an extraordinarily dense archive for the social history of Mithila, Vajji and Anga, but the archive must be read as a history of classification as well as a description of society. From Buchanan-Hamilton’s early district inquiries to the censuses, Risley’s ethnography, Grierson’s linguistic survey and the gazetteers, officials progressively standardized names, boundaries and comparative tables.

mai.title: औपनिवेशिक सर्वेक्षण आ सामाजिक श्रेणीक निर्माण
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “औपनिवेशिक सर्वेक्षण आ सामाजिक श्रेणीक निर्माण” विषयक राजस्व, व्यापार, कम्पनी शासन, नगदी फसल, अकाल, सर्वेक्षण, शिक्षा, मुद्रण, यातायात आ श्रमक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Colonial knowledge became an instrument of administration
The Company survey preceded the decennial census by decades
Buchanan-Hamilton’s method joined observation to local testimony
Early surveys mixed social, occupational and religious classifications

en.title: Education under Colonialism
en.summary: Colonial education transformed the institutional ecology of Mithila, Vajji and Anga by linking schools, examinations and credentials to a growing public and professional labour market. The change was cumulative rather than substitutive. Sanskrit ṭols, vernacular schools, maktabs, madrasas and household learning persisted while government schools, aided institutions, colleges and university examinations expanded.

mai.title: औपनिवेशिक शासनक अधीन शिक्षा
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “औपनिवेशिक शासनक अधीन शिक्षा” विषयक राजस्व, व्यापार, कम्पनी शासन, नगदी फसल, अकाल, सर्वेक्षण, शिक्षा, मुद्रण, यातायात आ श्रमक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Colonial education was a layered institutional transition
Indigenous learning remained visible in early nineteenth-century surveys
Ṭols, pāṭhśālās, maktabs and madrasas served different educational purposes
William Adam’s reports of 1835–38 are crucial evidence and require caution

en.title: Print Culture
en.summary: Print culture changed the social life of texts in Mithila, Vajji and Anga by making arguments, reports, literary works and linguistic claims reproducible across distance. It did not erase manuscript or oral transmission. Instead, presses, lithography, schools, postal systems, railways, journals and associations created a denser communication environment in which English, Hindi, Urdu, Maithili and Sanskrit occupied overlapping but unequal positions.

mai.title: मुद्रण-संस्कृति
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “मुद्रण-संस्कृति” विषयक राजस्व, व्यापार, कम्पनी शासन, नगदी फसल, अकाल, सर्वेक्षण, शिक्षा, मुद्रण, यातायात आ श्रमक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Print culture was an institutional ecology, not a single technological event
Manuscript, oral and printed transmission continued to coexist
Calcutta functioned as an external publishing metropolis for Bihar and Mithila
Government, missionary and commercial printing created different textual markets

en.title: Railways, Roads and Changing Markets
en.summary: Railways reorganized the economic geography of Mithila, Vajji and Anga without erasing rivers, roads, ferries or animal transport. South of the Ganga, the East Indian Railway reached major Anga towns in the early 1860s; north of the river, the Tirhut network expanded from famine-relief construction in the 1870s into a branching metre-gauge system. Stations and junctions changed market hierarchy, roads increasingly became railway feeders, and new links drew frontier trade toward railheads.

mai.title: रेल, सड़क आ बदलैत बजार
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “रेल, सड़क आ बदलैत बजार” विषयक राजस्व, व्यापार, कम्पनी शासन, नगदी फसल, अकाल, सर्वेक्षण, शिक्षा, मुद्रण, यातायात आ श्रमक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Transport change was a reordering of networks
Rivers remained economic infrastructure
Anga entered the railway era earlier than much of north Bihar
Jamalpur created an industrial railway node

en.title: Labour Migration
en.summary: Labour migration became one of the most consequential connections between the agrarian households of Mithila, Vajji and Anga and the expanding colonial economy. Yet there was no single migrant stream. Seasonal workers, circular urban migrants, railway and workshop labourers, plantation recruits, women moving within family labour strategies, and indentured emigrants faced different destinations and different degrees of freedom.

mai.title: श्रम-प्रवासन
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “श्रम-प्रवासन” विषयक राजस्व, व्यापार, कम्पनी शासन, नगदी फसल, अकाल, सर्वेक्षण, शिक्षा, मुद्रण, यातायात आ श्रमक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Labour migration was several mobilities, not one exodus
Agrarian pressure made mobility a household strategy
Flood, scarcity and the agricultural calendar shaped departure
Land, debt and social hierarchy shaped who could migrate

en.title: Women and Colonial Modernity
en.summary: Colonial modernity altered women’s lives in Mithila, Vajji and Anga through schools, law, print, medicine, labour markets, migration and nationalist politics, but the changes were profoundly unequal. Female literacy remained low even as girls’ education became an explicit field of policy; statutes changed the legal treatment of widow remarriage, consent and child marriage without ensuring uniform social compliance; hospitals and trained female personnel expanded without displacing household medicine; and political…

mai.title: महिला आ औपनिवेशिक आधुनिकता
mai.summary: ई अध्याय “महिला आ औपनिवेशिक आधुनिकता” विषयक राजस्व, व्यापार, कम्पनी शासन, नगदी फसल, अकाल, सर्वेक्षण, शिक्षा, मुद्रण, यातायात आ श्रमक स्रोत-आधारित ऐतिहासिक पड़ताल करैत अछि।

outline: Colonial modernity was uneven, layered and contested
The archive itself produces a gendered field of visibility
Household labour was an economic institution, not a private residue
Women’s agrarian work varied sharply by class, caste and locality
